subChunks.title: Variables, Primitives & Wrapper Classes
subChunks.hookHtml: Before a wizard can cast spells, they must understand the building blocks of magic — the containers that hold power. In Java, those containers are called variables.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Variables and Primitive Types

A variable is a named container that holds a value. Java is statically typed — every variable must be declared with a type before it can be used.

The Eight Primitive Types

byte   b = 127;           // -128 to 127
short  s = 32_000;        // -32,768 to 32,767
int    i = 2_000_000;     // most common whole-number type
long   l = 9_000_000_000L;// needs L suffix
float  f = 3.14f;         // needs f suffix, less precise
double d = 3.14159;       // default decimal type
boolean flag = true;      // only true or false
char   c = 'A';           // single Unicode character

Wrapper Classes

Each primitive has a wrapper class — an object version that lives in the standard library:

Integer count = 42;    // wraps int
Double  price = 9.99;  // wraps double
Boolean active = true; // wraps boolean

Wrappers are needed whenever an API requires an object (e.g., List<Integer> — you cannot write List<int>). Java autoboxes primitives to their wrappers automatically in most contexts, and unboxes them back:

Integer x = 5;    // autoboxing: int 5 → Integer
int     y = x;    // unboxing: Integer → int

Wrapper classes also offer useful utility methods: Integer.parseInt("42") converts a String to an int, Integer.MAX_VALUE gives the largest possible int, and Integer.toBinaryString(42) shows the binary representation.

String: Not a Primitive

String is a class, not a primitive, but it behaves like one in common usage:

String name = "Eldrin";          // string literal
String title = new String("Archmage"); // heap object (avoid)
System.out.println(name.length()); // 6
System.out.println(name.toUpperCase()); // ELDRIN

storyBeats.text: You arrive at the Arcane Academy's intake hall. Stone runes glow faintly on the walls. A stern-faced wizard in obsidian robes approaches, eyeing you the way a blacksmith eyes raw ore.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Apprentice. Before you learn a single spell, you must understand what magic is made of. Everything — every fireball, every portal, every ward — begins with a container. We call them runes. The rest of the world calls them variables.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Java has eight primitive types — the raw essences. int for whole numbers. double for decimals. boolean for truth and falsehood. char for a single glyph. Each is a specific shape of vessel that holds a specific kind of energy.

storyBeats.speaker: Declaring runes
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: But sometimes the Academy's records systems demand object vessels, not raw essence. For those moments, we have Wrapper Classes — Integer, Double, Boolean. Java can convert between primitive and wrapper automatically. We call this autoboxing.

storyBeats.speaker: Autoboxing in action
storyBeats.text:
Integer scrollCount = 5;   // autoboxed from int
int rolled = scrollCount;  // unboxed back to int
System.out.println(Integer.MAX_VALUE); // 2147483647

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Now, the most versatile rune of all — String. Not a primitive; a full class. But used so often it gets special treatment. Learn it well — it will be your constant companion.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
The Academy's intake scroll requires a new student profile. Declare the following variables and print each on its own line:

  • A String called wizardName set to "Lyria"
  • An int called level set to 1
  • A double called manaReserve set to 100.5
  • A boolean called enrolled set to true
  • An Integer wrapper called spellsLearned set to 0

Then print the maximum possible int value using Integer.MAX_VALUE.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between Java's eight primitive types and their wrapper classes. Why do wrapper classes exist, and when would you use Integer instead of int?

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Java automatically converts a primitive (e.g. int) to its wrapper class (e.g. Integer) when needed — and unboxes back the other way.
Named containers in memory that hold a value of a declared type. In Java every variable must be typed before use.
One of Java's 8 built-in value types: byte, short, int, long, float, double, boolean, char. Stored directly on the stack, not as heap objects.
Object versions of Java primitives (Integer, Double, Boolean, etc.) that allow primitives to be used in APIs requiring objects, such as collections.
A language property where every variable's type is known and checked at compile time, preventing type mismatches before the program runs.

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: The enrollment scroll is waiting — and this time there's no template to copy from. Declare Lyria's student profile entirely from memory: the five variables (wizardName, level, manaReserve, enrolled, and the Integer wrapper spellsLearned), print each on its own line, then print Integer.MAX_VALUE. No starter code, no hints — only what you've internalised.

questions.questionHtml: Which of the following is a primitive type in Java?
questions.explanationHtml: double is one of Java's eight primitive types. String, Integer, and Character are all classes (objects).
Java generics only work with reference types (objects). You must use the wrapper class: List<Integer>. The compiler then autoboxes values for you.

questions.questionHtml: Which primitive type holds a single character in Java?
questions.explanationHtml: char holds a single Unicode character, e.g. char c = 'A';. String (a class) holds multiple characters. Character is the wrapper class for char.

questions.questionHtml: Java's byte type can hold values from -256 to 255.
questions.explanationHtml: byte is an 8-bit signed integer and holds values from -128 to 127. The range -256 to 255 is a common misconception — that would require 9 bits.

questions.questionHtml: What suffix is required when assigning a long literal that exceeds int range?
questions.explanationHtml: Long literals larger than Integer.MAX_VALUE require the L suffix (e.g. long x = 9_000_000_000L;). Without it the compiler treats it as an int literal and reports an overflow error.
Integer a = 100 autoboxes. int b = a unboxes. Then b + 1 is normal int arithmetic giving 101.
Integer.MIN_VALUE is the smallest possible int value: −231 = −2,147,483,648.

questions.questionHtml: A developer writes double price = 9.99f;. What is stored in price?
options: double, but precision may differ from 9.99
questions.correctAnswer: double, but precision may differ from 9.99
questions.explanationHtml: The float literal 9.99f is widened to double, but float has less precision, so the stored value may not be exactly 9.99. Always use a double literal (e.g. 9.99) when assigning to a double.

questions.questionHtml: Which method converts a String to an int in Java?
questions.explanationHtml: Integer.parseInt("42") parses a String and returns an int. Integer.valueOf("42") returns an Integer object. The cast (int) str does not compile.

questions.questionHtml: A developer writes: Integer count = null; int value = count; — what happens at runtime?
questions.explanationHtml: Unboxing a null Integer calls intValue() on a null reference, throwing a NullPointerException. Always null-check wrapper types before unboxing, or use Objects.requireNonNullElse(count, 0).

options: For simple arithmetic — int is faster and uses less memory
Integer should always be used for clarity
int cannot be null so it is always safer regardless of context
questions.correctAnswer: For simple arithmetic — int is faster and uses less memory
questions.explanationHtml: Primitives avoid object overhead and are stored on the stack. Use Integer when you need null-ability, generics (List<Integer>), or utility methods like Integer.parseInt(). For plain arithmetic, int is always preferred.

subChunks.title: Operators & Operator Precedence
subChunks.hookHtml: A wizard who casts spells in the wrong order risks catastrophe. Java expressions follow strict rules about which operations happen first — master operator precedence or face unpredictable results.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Arithmetic Operators

int a = 17, b = 5;
System.out.println(a + b);  // 22 — addition
System.out.println(a - b);  // 12 — subtraction
System.out.println(a * b);  // 85 — multiplication
System.out.println(a / b);  // 3  — integer division (truncates!)
System.out.println(a % b);  // 2  — modulo (remainder)

Comparison & Logical Operators

boolean eq  = (a == b); // false — equality
boolean neq = (a != b); // true  — not equal
boolean gt  = (a > b);  // true  — greater than
boolean and = (a > 0 && b > 0); // true — both conditions
boolean or  = (a < 0 || b > 0); // true — at least one
boolean not = !(a == b);        // true — negation

Compound Assignment

int x = 10;
x += 5;  // x = 15
x -= 3;  // x = 12
x *= 2;  // x = 24
x /= 4;  // x = 6
x %= 4;  // x = 2

Increment & Decrement

int n = 5;
System.out.println(n++); // prints 5, then n becomes 6 (post)
System.out.println(++n); // n becomes 7, then prints 7 (pre)

Operator Precedence (high → low)

  1. ++ -- (postfix), then ++ -- (prefix), !
  2. * / %
  3. + -
  4. < > <= >=
  5. == !=
  6. &&
  7. ||
  8. = += -= etc.

When in doubt, use parentheses: (a + b) * c is always clear.

storyBeats.text: Eldrin draws a complex rune diagram on the chalkboard — nested circles within circles, each with small symbols connecting them.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Magic is applied in sequence. 3 + 4 * 2 — do you add first, or multiply first? If you said multiply, you are correct. Multiplication has higher precedence than addition. The result is 11, not 14.

storyBeats.speaker: Precedence trap
storyBeats.text:
int wrong = 3 + 4 * 2; // 11 (not 14!)
int clear = (3 + 4) * 2; // 14 — parentheses win

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Now for the subtlest trick — post-increment versus pre-increment. n++ returns the current value, then increments. ++n increments first, then returns. Many apprentices have lost marks on exams over this.

storyBeats.speaker: Pre vs post increment
storyBeats.text:
int n = 5;
System.out.println(n++); // 5 (returns 5, then n→6)
System.out.println(n);   // 6
System.out.println(++n); // 7 (increments first, then returns 7)

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And the modulo operator — % — gives you the remainder after division. Use it to test if a number is even (n % 2 == 0), to wrap indices around an array, or to extract digits. It is more useful than you might think.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Calculate and print the following three values:

  1. The result of 3 + 4 * 2 - 1 (follow normal precedence, no extra parentheses)
  2. The remainder of 29 % 6
  3. Starting with int score = 10, apply score += 5 then score *= 2 and print the final score
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain Java operator precedence to a friend. Include an example where getting the order wrong produces a surprising answer, and explain how to avoid the problem.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
An alchemist needs three quick calculations for their potion lab. Write the code from scratch — no starter this time:

  1. A basic recipe requires 3 * 4 - 8 / 4 drops of essence. Print the result — watch your precedence, both * and / bind before -.
  2. The alchemist has 35 moonflower petals split evenly into bags of 6. Print the remainder left over using %.
  3. Start with int gold = 20. Deduct 5 for ingredients (gold -= 5), then double the result by selling the finished potion (gold *= 2). Print the final amount.

questions.explanationHtml: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition. 3 * 4 = 12, then 2 + 12 = 14.
When both operands are integers, Java performs integer division and truncates the decimal. 7 / 2 = 3. Use 7.0 / 2 or (double) 7 / 2 to get 3.5.

options: The result rounded to the nearest integer
The fractional part of the division
questions.explanationHtml: % is the modulo operator. 17 % 5 = 2 because 17 = 3 × 5 + 2. It's useful for detecting even/odd numbers, cycling through array indices, and extracting digits.
++n is the pre-increment operator — it increments n by 1 before any other operation. After ++n, n is 11, so println prints 11.
n++ returns the current value of n first, then increments it. Pre-increment (++n) increments first and then returns the new value.
n++ (post-increment) returns the current value (5) before incrementing. After the statement, n is 6.
17 / 5 = 3 remainder 2. The % operator returns the remainder.
x -= 3 sets x = 5. Then x *= 2 sets x = 10. Compound operators modify the variable in place, applying in sequence.

questions.questionHtml: A developer wants to check if a number is odd. What is wrong with this condition?
questions.correctAnswer: It fails for negative odd numbers, where n % 2 is -1, not 1. Use n % 2 != 0 instead.
questions.explanationHtml: In Java, the sign of the result of % matches the sign of the left operand. So -3 % 2 is -1, not 1. The safe idiom for odd-check is n % 2 != 0.

questions.correctAnswer: ArithmeticException — integer division by zero throws an exception
questions.explanationHtml: Integer division by zero throws java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero at runtime. Note: floating-point division by zero does not throw — it produces Infinity or NaN (e.g. 5.0 / 0 = Infinity).

questions.questionHtml: A developer wants to toggle a boolean flag. Which is the cleanest approach?
options: if (flag) flag = false; else flag = true;
questions.explanationHtml: flag = !flag uses the logical NOT operator for a clean, idiomatic toggle. flag ^= true works but is less readable. The if/else is unnecessarily verbose. flag = flag == false also works but reads awkwardly.
